newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. envoy wants Afghan ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy wants Afghan ceasefire.

text.p: A U.N. special envoy said on Wednesday an end to bloodshed in Afghanistan was a top priority as he prepared for fresh talks with an Afghan alliance opposed to the Taleban movement.

Envoy Norbert Holl, due to leave on Thursday for the opposition-held northern Aghan town of Mazar-i-Sharif, held talks on Wednesday with a senior Pakistan foreign ministry official, Iftikhar Murshed, who is engaged in Islamabad's own peace initiative in Afghanistan.

Holl, speaking to Pakistan state television, made clear that all peace efforts must be under the U.N. umbrella and that he regarded a ceasefire between the dominant Taleban Islamic movement and its opponents as the first priority.

"Tomorrow, I will go to Mazar to find out how the prospects are, because one thing is clear -- it is clear for the Pakistan government, it is clear for myself -- that all the peace efforts shall be undertaken under the auspices of the United Nations," he said.
"I think the first step to be taken indeed is a ceasefire because the bloodshed has to end," Holl said when asked about the agenda of his talks with the opposition alliance based in Mazar-i-Sharif.

In a related development, Taleban movement chief mullah Omar issued a statement on Wednesday warning the opposition alliance of dire consequences if it harmed hundreds of Taleban fighters and several officials held prisoner in Mazar-i-Sharif.
The statement, quoted by a Pakistan-based Afghan news service, asked the opposition alliance to release the prisoners or provide them with full security.
"If it is not done, those holding the prisoners will be responsible for the dire consequences they will face," the Afghan Islamic Press quoted the statement as saying.
Murshed met Taleban officials in the southern Afghan town of Kandahar for about four hours on Tuesday and later called his talks a step forward.

Murshed last met Afghan opposition leader General Abdul Malik in Mazar-i-Sharif on July 1 after talks with Taleban officials in Kandahar, and later said he had found the two sides far apart to make peace.
The opposition alliance had proposed demilitarisation of the Taleban-held capital Kabul and formation of a political commission to chart the outlines of a broad-based government.
The Taleban agree to forming the commission but have refused to demilitarise Kabul, which they captured in September.
They also want a ceasefire and the release of their prisoners as pre-conditions for peace talks, which Pakistan has offered to host in Islamabad.

Pakistan recognised the Taleban government in late May, after the purist Islamic militia briefly captured Mazar-i-Sharif with Malik's help, and was followed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Malik turned on the Taleban at the end of May, linking up with a Shi'ite Moslem Hezb-i-Wahdat faction to drive them from Mazar-i-Sharif.
